title: Microburst and Mixed-Concurrency Harness Design for Throughput Benchmarks
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures a focused design for a throughput benchmarking harness that emphasizes: microburst sensitivity, mixed-concurrency workloads (multi-tenant/multi-model mixes), repeatability across runs, and practical warmup/priming heuristics. The goal: give engineering teams a reproducible recipe and a set of configs to evaluate production-like tail behavior and steady-state throughput in the serving runtime.

High-level goals (quick):
- Measure steady-state throughput under realistic mixes (short+long sequences, embedding+generation).
- Surface microburst-induced queueing and head-of-line effects that break latency SLOs.
- Ensure runs are repeatable: seedable randoms, deterministic schedule export, and artifact capture (metrics/logs).
- Provide warmup and priming rules to avoid transient, misleading throughput numbers.

Definitions (how we use terms here):
- microburst: a short-duration spike of requests (ms-to-seconds) with higher-than-average concurrency or token-length.
- mixed-concurrency workload: concurrent streams with different request templates, token lengths, and required batchability.
- priming: backend-level priming to populate KV caches, JIT/kernels, and DLL loads before measurement window.
- warmup: sustained traffic used to reach steady runtime scheduling and kernel warm paths.

Design overview (phases of a run):
1) Environment prep (pre-checks)
   - Ensure GPU driver, CUDA, and runtime metrics agent are stable.
   - Clear device caches if testing cold-starts (documented scripts below).
   - Pin model versions and quantization profile.
   - Start telemetry collectors (Prometheus exporters, nvml daemon, runtime trace).
2) Priming phase (short, targeted priming, 1-3 min)
   - Hit the model with 5–20 unique long-sequence requests to fill KV caches and warm kernels that depend on non-trivial sequence lengths.
   - Purpose: avoid first-request penalties; we treat priming artifacts separate from warmup.
3) Warmup phase (sustained ramp, 5–30 min depending on model/hardware)
   - Controlled ramp: start at 10% target concurrency, double every 60s until 80% of target.
   - Hold at target for a minimum warmup window: see heuristics below.
4) Measurement window (steady-state)
   - Fixed-duration windows (recommended 10 minutes min for stable estimate). Capture per-second and per-request telemetry.
   - Run multiple windows (3+) separated by short cool-downs to check stability across windows.
5) Cool-down and teardown
   - Decrease traffic gradually to avoid sudden kernel evictions or scheduling artifacts for subsequent runs.

Warmup heuristics (rule-of-thumb):
- Small models (<8GB): warmup 5–10 minutes after ramping to target concurrency.
- Medium models (8–30GB): 10–20 minutes; check GPU SM & memory bandwidth stabilization.
- Large models (>30GB): 20–30 minutes; also verify any host-side paging/allocator behavior is steady.
- Stability trigger: compute coefficient of variation (CoV) on 1s throughput for the last 5 minutes; require CoV < 3% for the run to be considered warmed.

Microburst-specific tests (why these matter):
- Bursts of short requests can starve long-running high-token requests in batch scheduling: test 1) short-only burst into baseline, 2) long-only burst, 3) mixed burst where 20% long requests join a short-heavy baseline.
- Burst profiles: 100ms, 500ms, 2s, 10s durations with intensity multipliers (x2, x5, x10).
- Observe queue length, scheduling latency, kernel launch latencies, and tail latency (p95/p99/p999).

Load generator configs (examples)
- We expect loadgen to support: seeded RNG for reproducibility, schedule export, poisson/exponential inter-arrival, deterministic burst patterns, concurrency groups, and per-template token-length distributions.
- Example compact config (YAML-like string used by our harness):

load_profile: mixed_microburst_test
seed: 123456
concurrency_targets:
  baseline_group:
    users: 100
    template_mix: 
      short: 0.7
      long: 0.2
      embedding: 0.1
    per_user_rate_rps: 0.05
  burst_group:
    users: 200
    schedule:
      - at: 00:02:00  # 2m into the run
        action: ramp_to
        target_users: 200
        duration: 00:00:10
        multiplier: 5
interarrival_dist: poisson
token_length_distributions:
  short: {mean: 16, sigma: 6}
  long: {mean: 512, sigma: 64}
measurement_window: 600 # seconds
export_trace: true

Repeatability checklist (must-haves):
- Single source of truth for the load profile (store config git commit + seed).
- Capture run artifacts: loadgen command, schedule export, Prometheus scrape (start/end), nvml logs, runtime logs (per-request traces if enabled), kernel trace (nsys/nsight) if investigating variance.
- Use consistent host/driver stack; record: CUDA version, driver, OS kernel, container image digest.
- Run at least three replicated experiments spaced across different times of day to detect noisy neighbors.
- Use run_id pattern: bench-<profile>-<date>-<seed>-<runindex>. Example: bench-microburst-20250212-123456-01

Metrics to capture (minimal):
- Per-request: latency (q, s, e phases if possible), bytes_in, bytes_out, template_id, request_id, gpu_mem_before/after
- Aggregates: rps, tokens/s, batch_size distribution, p50/p90/p95/p99/p999 latencies, error rate, throttle events
- Hardware: GPU util, SM occupancy, memory bandwidth, PCIe throughput, CPU run queue length, network egress (if remote model).
- Runtime internals (if exposed): batcher queue length, batch coalescing rate, KV cache hit ratio, kernel launch count, time spent in copy vs compute.

Analysis and acceptance criteria:
- Acceptable steady-state throughput: median tokens/s within 5% across replicate runs AND CoV < 4% on 1s throughput samples.
- Tail safety: p99 latency must not exceed configured SLO by >20% under tested bursts. If violated, document gating behavior (auto-fallbacks, drop policies).
- Microburst safety: after a burst, 99th percentile latency should return to baseline within a defined cool-down (recommended 2x burst duration) without persistent queuing backlog.

Instrumentation tips (how to quickly get the right traces):
- Short investigations: enable Prometheus + per-request logs at INFO for 1 window. Set request sampling to 1% to keep volume manageable.
- Deep investigations: use nsys on a representative instance; capture a 2–4 minute segment that overlaps the burst. Capture host perf counters for the same window.
- For Triton deployments: enable Triton GPU metrics and backend timing. Correlate Triton’s batch queue length with runtime-level batcher metrics.

Practical commands (examples)
- run harness (pseudo): ./bench-runner --profile mixed_microburst_test --seed 123456 --out artifacts/bench-microburst-20250212-123456-01
- export schedule: ./bench-runner schedule export --profile mixed_microburst_test --out schedule.json
- start nsys capture (example): nsys profile --output artifacts/nsys-microburst.qdrep --trace=cuda,cudnn --duration=180s -- ./bench-runner ...

Quick experiment templates (what to run first):
1) Baseline steady-state throughput with only short templates at target concurrency. Confirm stable tokens/s and CoV < 3%.
2) Single microburst: at t=120s trigger x5 short request burst for 10s. Measure immediate tail.
3) Mixed burst: 80% short baseline + inject 20% long burst (512 tokens) at x2 for 30s — check p99 and batch size shift.
4) Repeatability run: re-run template 2 and 3 three times with same seed and compare per-second throughput.

Unresolved items / notes to self (for follow-ups):
- Need a compact mechanism to share schedule artifacts across teams (S3 + git pointer?).
- Investigate whether NVLink congestion shows up in our perf counters for multi-GPU pods; plan a targeted test.
- How to standardize sampling of per-request traces without overwhelming logging? Consider adaptive sampling tied to tail events.

Practical pitfalls we've seen (short list):
- Too-short measurement windows (under 2m) report overly optimistic throughput after warmup artifacts; prefer >=10m.
- Running back-to-back without cool-down sometimes leaves allocator state in an unrepresentative condition.
- Burst ramps that are instantaneous (0s) create kernel-latch effects that rarely occur in prod; prefer small ramp (5–10s) to be realistic.

Appendix: small reproducible config example (JSON for bench-runner interop)
{
  "profile": "microburst_smoke",
  "seed": "20250212-999",
  "duration": 900,
  "concurrency": [50, 200],
  "burst_events": [
    {"t": 120, "type": "ramp", "to_concurrency": 250, "over_secs": 10},
    {"t": 220, "type": "drop", "to_concurrency": 50, "over_secs": 5}
  ],
  "templates": [
    {"id": "short", "mean_tokens": 16, "weight": 0.75},
    {"id": "long", "mean_tokens": 512, "weight": 0.25}
  ]
}

If you take anything from this doc: start with a 3-phase run (priming, warmup, measurement) and record the seed+schedule. For microbursts, model the ramp shape; instantaneous jumps rarely reflect realistic traffic and will mask how the batcher coalesces.

If we want to turn this into a shared PRD: next step is to convert key configs into bench-runner-compatible YAMLs, add schedule export hooks, and create a lightweight artifact registry for run metadata (S3 prefix + json manifest).

End of note.
